title: Defaults and definite assignment
hook: Fields start at `default`. Locals do not — the compiler demands definite assignment. That difference catches bugs JS `undefined` would silently leak.

sections.heading: default(T) versus unassigned locals
sections.prose: Every type has a default: `0` for numeric, `false` for `bool`, `null` for reference types and `Nullable<T>`, all-zero fields for structs. Fields, array elements, and `new T()` for a class get those defaults. Local variables must be assigned on every path before read — “definite assignment.” `int n; Console.WriteLine(n);` is a compile error, not `undefined`. `default` or `default(int)` is the explicit spelling. In a CSV importer, a missing field should be an explicit `default` or a nullable, not an unassigned local you hope is zero.

snippets.label: Wrong unassigned local vs right default
snippets.explanation: Fields on a class are zeroed by the runtime. Locals are not. Do not copy JS habits of declaring then filling inside branches without an else.

interviewTakeaways: Definite assignment is a compile-time rule for locals (and `out` parameters).
`default` for a reference type is `null`; for `int` it is `0`.
Structs’ fields default independently; a struct local still must be fully assigned before use unless you `= default`.
commonPitfalls: Reading a field and assuming a local works the same.
Using `default` for `string` in an NRT context and ignoring the warning (module 07).
Partial assignment of a struct local (`p.X = 1` without `p.Y`) still failing definite assignment.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS locals are `undefined` until set. C# refuses to read them. TS `strictPropertyInitialization` is the closest analog for class fields.
